newsitem.title: SPAIN: Madrid's makeshift airport crawls into action.
newsitem.headline: Madrid's makeshift airport crawls into action.

text.p: Madrid's second airport opened for business on Monday ready to relieve traffic from the capital's overstretched Barajas airport, but found itself lacking airlines willing to use its runways.

A series of near disasters at Madrid's main airport last year forced the government to introduce measures to ease overcrowding which included using the local Torrejon military airbase to receive some flights.
But airlines have been frightened off by a lack of facilities at Torrejon and have refused to transfer their flights from the main airport.
By the inauguration on Monday just one airline of the 120 that operate out of Barajas had agreed to use the former U.S. military airbase -- Air Truck.
"There are negotiations going on, but so far no other companies are interested in using Torrejon, only Air Truck," said Ivan Tejada, an official from Spanish airport authority AENA.

AENA has spent 300 million pesetas ($2.1 million) converting part of the military airbase for civilian use. But on Monday the only rumble of engines came from two Air Truck flights and the sparkling new buildings stood deserted.
"Torrejon is not the solution for Madrid's problems, it is just a temporary solution," Air Truck's chairman Gerardo Herrero told reporters at the airbase.
"The solution is in the third runway that is being built at Barajas...what Madrid needs is an airport capacity of at least 120 flights an hour," he added.
The government has awarded a contract to build a third runway but construction will take almost two years.
In the meantime, Barajas has a capacity to receive just 50 flights an hour, while Torrejon can receive a further five.
"Even after the third runway is built, if traffic continues to increase as it has been we will definitely need a new airport," said a spokesman from state airline Iberia.
Barajas, Spain's busiest airport with around 20 million passengers a year, has been struggling with an increasing amount of air traffic in recent months.
Some officials doubted Torrejon would relieve the main airport's congestion, adding so little capacity and with such limited facilities.

Airlines also pointed out that only a handful of passenger flights qualified to land at Torrejon. The Defence Ministry has said only turbopropelled aircraft with capacity for less than 70 passengers are authorised to use the military base.
For one elegible airline, Air Nostrum, transfer time problems were the key hindrance to using the airbase.
"Air Nostrum has many connecting flights that wouldn't be possible if we moved to Torrejon, and the facilities are not good enough for our passengers," an Air Nostrum spokesman said.

The Development Ministry said it had started to build a connecting road between the two airports to help reduce transfer times but for the meantime passengers and luggage must be ferried by coach along the busy motorways.
The added burden of having to check-in and pick up luggage at Barajas also increased travelling time unacceptably, airlines added.
